title: Levers and Torque
bigQuestion: How can one quick stomp on the tail lift the whole front of a skateboard into the air?

story.title: The Ruler on the Desk
story.kicker: A tapped ruler leaps off a desk, and a seventh grader sees a skateboard in it.
paragraphs: Mr. Okafor sets a wooden ruler on the edge of his desk. About a third of it sticks out past the edge. A pink eraser sits on the far end, resting on the desk. He asks the class to guess what will happen when he taps the end that hangs in the air.

He brings his finger down fast on the overhanging end. The ruler tips over the edge of the desk like a seesaw. The far end jumps up, and the eraser flies toward the ceiling. It lands in the front row, and a student named Dani catches it.

Dani turns the eraser over in her hand. She skates every weekend at the park near her house. "That is an ollie," she says. "The desk edge is like my back wheels. The part you tapped is my tail." Mr. Okafor writes two words on the board: lever and torque.

He taps the ruler again, this time close to the desk edge. The far end barely moves, and the eraser only wobbles. Then he taps the very tip of the overhang. The eraser flies higher than before. The class starts to argue about why the same tap works so differently in different places.

Dani grabs her board from her locker and sets it on the carpet. She presses the tail down slowly with her hand. The nose rises while the back wheels stay on the floor. "Same thing," she says. "Now we just need to figure out the numbers."
story.think: Why did tapping the very tip of the ruler send the eraser higher than tapping near the desk edge?

lessons.title: What a Lever Does
lessons.mainIdea: A lever is a stiff bar that turns around a fixed point, so a push on one side moves the other side.
reading: A playground seesaw is the easiest lever to picture. It is a long, stiff board resting on a bar in the middle. When one rider pushes down, the board turns around the bar, and the other rider goes up. A *lever* is any stiff bar that turns around one fixed point. Crowbars, scissors and bottle openers are levers too.

The fixed point a lever turns around is the *fulcrum*. On a seesaw the fulcrum is the bar in the middle. On Mr. Okafor's ruler it was the edge of the desk. Every part of the lever swings around the fulcrum at the same time. When one end goes down, the other end must go up.

A lever has two other parts worth naming. The *effort* is the push you put in. The load is the thing being moved, such as the eraser or the other rider. Scientists study levers because they change how a push works. A small push in the right spot can move a heavy load, or a short motion can become a long one.

words.d: a stiff bar that turns around one fixed point
the fixed point a lever turns around; also called the pivot
the push or pull a person puts into a lever

look.title: A Seesaw in Slow Motion
look.text: Picture a seesaw with a friend on each end. The bar in the middle does not move. One friend pushes off the ground and goes up. At the very same moment, the other friend sinks down. The board never bends; it just turns around the bar.
look.prompt: Point to the fulcrum, the effort and the load on this seesaw. Then find the same three parts on a pair of scissors.

check.q: What is a fulcrum?
choices: The heaviest end of a lever
The fixed point a lever turns around
The push a person gives a lever
check.why: The fulcrum is the fixed point, like the bar under a seesaw, that the lever turns around.

check.q: On Mr. Okafor's ruler, what acted as the fulcrum?
choices: The far end of the ruler
check.why: The ruler turned around the edge of the desk, so the edge was the fulcrum.

check.q: When one end of a stiff lever goes down, what does the other end do?
check.why: A stiff lever turns as one piece around the fulcrum, so the far end rises.

lessons.title: Finding the Pivot on a Board
lessons.mainIdea: When the tail is pressed down, a skateboard turns around its rear wheels, so the rear wheels are the fulcrum.
reading: Set a skateboard on a carpet or on grass, where it cannot roll away. Put your hand on the *tail*, the short end that bends up behind the back wheels. Press down slowly. The tail sinks, the back wheels stay on the floor, and the *nose* at the front lifts into the air.

The board just acted like Mr. Okafor's ruler. It turned around the place where the rear wheels touch the ground. That makes the rear wheels the fulcrum, or *pivot*, of the skateboard lever. The tail is on one side of the pivot. The rest of the board, with the front wheels and the nose, is on the other side.

This is the first thing that happens in an *ollie*, the jump where a skater and board rise together with no hands. The back foot presses the tail, the board turns around the rear wheels, and the nose comes up. Everything else in the ollie builds on this simple lever.

words.d: the back end of the deck, behind the rear wheels, usually bent upward
the front end of the deck, ahead of the front wheels
the point something turns around; on a board pressed at the tail, the rear wheels
a jump in which the skater and board leave the ground together without using hands

look.title: The Hand Test
look.text: A board rests on a carpet. A hand presses the tail down, little by little. The rear wheels stay touching the carpet the whole time. The front wheels lift off first, then the nose rises higher and higher. When the tail touches the carpet, the board stops turning.
look.prompt: Try the hand test with a real board on carpet or grass. Which wheels stay on the ground, and what stops the nose from rising any higher?

check.q: When you press the tail down, which part of the board stays on the ground and acts as the pivot?
check.why: The board turns around the rear wheels, so they stay down and act as the pivot.

check.q: Why should you test this on carpet or grass first?
choices: The board cannot roll away there
check.why: On carpet or grass the wheels do not roll, so the board stays put while you study it.

check.q: What is an ollie?
choices: Pressing the nose to spin the board
Turning on the back wheels only
A jump where skater and board rise together with no hands
check.why: An ollie is a no-hands jump in which the board rises with the skater.

lessons.title: Small Push, Big Swing
lessons.mainIdea: Points far from the pivot move farther than points close to it, so a short drop of the tail makes a big rise of the nose.
reading: Watch two dots on a turning lever. One dot is near the fulcrum, and one is far away. Both dots turn through the same angle at the same time. But the far dot travels a much longer path. On a lever, the farther a point is from the pivot, the farther it moves.

A skateboard uses this. The tail is short, and the nose is far from the rear wheels. Here is a worked example with example lengths. Say the tail tip is 0.15 m behind the rear wheels and the nose tip is 0.53 m in front of them. The nose is 0.53 ÷ 0.15, or about 3.5 times, as far from the pivot.

For small turns, each point moves in proportion to its distance from the pivot. So if the tail tip drops 5 cm, the nose tip rises about 5 × 3.5 = 17.5 cm. A short stomp at the back becomes a big lift at the front. That lift is the *ratio* of the two distances at work, and it is why the ollie starts with the tail.

words.d: how many times bigger one number is than another, found by dividing
a relationship where one amount grows by the same factor as another

look.title: Two Chalk Marks
look.text: Put one chalk mark on a board's tail tip and one on its nose tip. Press the tail until the tail mark drops the width of two fingers. Now look at the nose mark. It has climbed much higher, about three and a half times as far, because it sits about three and a half times farther from the rear wheels.
look.prompt: If the tail tip dropped 4 cm and the nose was 3.5 times as far from the pivot, about how far would the nose tip rise? Show your multiplication.

check.q: On a turning lever, which point moves farthest?
choices: The point farthest from the fulcrum
The point closest to the fulcrum
Every point moves the same distance
check.why: All points turn through the same angle, so the point farthest from the fulcrum travels the longest path.

check.q: In the worked example, the nose tip is 0.53 m from the pivot and the tail tip is 0.15 m. About how many times farther is the nose?
check.why: 0.53 ÷ 0.15 is about 3.5, so the nose is about 3.5 times as far from the pivot.

check.q: If the tail tip drops 5 cm and the ratio is 3.5, about how far does the nose tip rise?
check.why: 5 cm × 3.5 = 17.5 cm, because the nose moves in proportion to its distance from the pivot.

lessons.title: What Torque Means
lessons.mainIdea: Torque is how strongly a force turns something, and it equals the force times its distance from the pivot.
reading: Try to open a heavy door by pushing right next to the hinges. It barely moves. Push the same door near the handle, far from the hinges, and it swings open easily. The push was the same size both times. What changed was the distance between your push and the turning point.

That turning effect has a name: *torque*. Torque tells how strongly a force makes something rotate around a pivot. It depends on two things: the size of the force and how far from the pivot the force acts. That distance is called the *lever arm*. A bigger force or a longer lever arm both give more torque.

Scientists write the rule as torque = force × lever arm. Force is measured in newtons (N), and the lever arm in meters (m). So torque is measured in *newton-meters*, written N·m. A push of 20 N on a door handle 0.8 m from the hinges gives a torque of 20 × 0.8 = 16 N·m. The same push 0.1 m from the hinges gives only 20 × 0.1 = 2 N·m.

words.d: the turning effect of a force; force times its distance from the pivot
the distance from the pivot to the place where a force pushes, measured straight across
the unit of torque, written N·m: newtons of force times meters of lever arm

look.title: The Door Test
look.text: Stand at a classroom door. Push with one finger right beside the hinges. Then push with the same finger at the edge near the handle. Your finger presses about the same both times, but only the second push swings the door. The longer lever arm made more torque.
look.prompt: Try the door test gently. Then explain, using the words torque and lever arm, why door handles are put far from the hinges.

check.q: What two things does torque depend on?
choices: The color and size of the object
The force and its distance from the pivot
The speed and weight of the object
The force and the time it lasts
check.why: Torque = force × lever arm, so it depends on the force and how far from the pivot it acts.

check.q: A 20 N push acts 0.8 m from a door's hinges. What is the torque?
check.why: Torque = 20 N × 0.8 m = 16 N·m.

check.q: Why does pushing a door near the hinges barely move it?
choices: The lever arm is very short, so the torque is small
The hinges push back harder there
The door is heavier near the hinges
Force does not work near a pivot
check.why: Near the hinges the lever arm is short, so the same force makes only a small torque.

lessons.title: Tail Tip or Bolts?
lessons.mainIdea: The same stomp makes far more torque on the tip of the tail than near the rear bolts, because the lever arm is longer.
reading: A skater's back foot can stand in different places. The *bolts* are the screw heads on top of the deck that hold each truck on. The rear bolts sit just a few centimeters from the rear wheels. The tail tip is much farther back. Where the back foot presses changes how much torque it makes around the rear wheels.

Here is a worked example with example numbers. Say the back foot stomps down with 400 N, about the weight of a 41 kg person, because 41 kg × 9.8 m/s² is about 400 N. Near the bolts, the lever arm might be 0.03 m. Torque = 400 N × 0.03 m = 12 N·m. On the tail tip, the lever arm might be 0.15 m. Torque = 400 N × 0.15 m = 60 N·m.

The same foot and the same stomp give five times the torque on the tail tip, because 60 ÷ 12 = 5. That is why skaters put the ball of the back foot on the end of the tail for an ollie. A skater who stands on the rear bolts and stomps will feel the board barely tip, just like the door pushed near its hinges.

words.d: the screw heads on top of the deck that hold the trucks on; a common way to describe where to stand
the padded part of the sole just behind the toes

look.title: Same Stomp, Different Spots
look.cite: Worked example: a 400 N stomp, torque = force × lever arm
look.prompt: What happens to the torque each time the foot moves 0.03 m farther back? Why does the table go up by the same amount each row?

check.q: A 400 N stomp lands 0.15 m from the rear wheels. What torque does it make?
check.why: Torque = 400 N × 0.15 m = 60 N·m.

check.q: Where should the back foot press for the biggest torque in an ollie?
choices: On the ball of the foot at the end of the tail
In the middle of the deck
check.why: The tail tip has the longest lever arm from the rear wheels, so it gives the most torque.

check.q: Why is a stomp near the rear bolts weak for an ollie?
choices: The front wheels are too far away
The lever arm from the rear wheels is very short
The stomp is a different force there
check.why: The rear bolts are only a few centimeters from the rear wheels, so the lever arm and the torque are small.

lessons.title: Torques That Fight
lessons.mainIdea: The front foot makes a torque the other way, so it must go light at the pop or the nose will not rise.
reading: A seesaw balances when the torques on its two sides are equal. A 300 N child sitting 2 m from the middle makes 300 × 2 = 600 N·m. A 400 N child sitting 1.5 m from the middle makes 400 × 1.5 = 600 N·m. The torques are equal and opposite, so the seesaw stays level. If one side's torque gets bigger, that side goes down.

A skateboard works the same way, with the rear wheels as the middle. The back foot on the tail turns the board one way. The front foot, standing ahead of the rear wheels, turns it the other way. Say the front foot presses 200 N at a spot 0.30 m from the rear wheels, just behind the front bolts. That is 200 × 0.30 = 60 N·m against the tail.

That 60 N·m exactly cancels the 60 N·m stomp from the last lesson, and the nose would not rise at all. So in an ollie the front foot must go light at the moment the back foot snaps. The skater does this by starting to jump and lifting the front knee. The tail's torque then wins, and the nose swings up.

words.d: when the torques on both sides of a pivot are equal, so nothing turns
a torque that tries to turn something the other way

look.title: How Hard the Front Foot Presses
look.cite: Worked example: front foot 0.30 m from the rear wheels, torque = force × lever arm
look.prompt: The tail stomp makes 60 N·m. In which rows would the nose still rise? What does that tell the front foot to do?

check.q: A 400 N child sits 1.5 m from the middle of a seesaw. What torque does that child make?
check.why: Torque = 400 N × 1.5 m = 600 N·m.

check.q: Why must the front foot go light at the moment of the pop?
choices: So its torque does not cancel the tail's torque
So the back foot can slide
So the tail does not touch the ground
check.why: The front foot's torque works against the tail. If it presses hard, it cancels the tail's torque and the nose stays down.

check.q: How does a skater make the front foot light at the pop?
choices: By leaning back over the tail
By starting to jump and lifting the front knee
By pushing with the front foot
check.why: Starting the jump and lifting the front knee takes weight off the front foot, so the tail's torque wins.

lessons.title: Flat Boards Came First
lessons.mainIdea: Early skateboards were mostly flat, and the upturned kicktail later gave skaters a lever they could press.
reading: The first skateboards of the late 1950s were often homemade: a plank with roller-skate wheels nailed or bolted underneath. Store-made boards appeared around 1959. Companies such as Makaha, started by Larry Stevenson in 1963, and Hobie sold boards in the 1960s. Most of these early decks were flat from end to end.

On a flat board, the back end is still a lever, but it is hard to use. The tail sits low and flat, so it has little room to swing down before it touches the ground. Skaters of the 1960s did tricks such as handstands, walking the board and spinning on the back wheels. They did not do ollies.

Larry Stevenson was granted a U.S. patent for a *kicktail* in 1971. A kicktail is a tail that bends upward at the back of the deck. It gave the back foot a clear place to press and turned the end of the board into a handy lever. Today most decks turn up at both ends, with a kicked nose as well as a kicked tail.

words.d: a tail that bends upward at the back of the deck so the foot can press it like a lever
the flat board a skater stands on
a government record that names an inventor and protects an invention for a set time

look.title: Two Boards Side by Side
look.text: On the left of a table lies a 1960s-style board: flat from nose to tail, with the wheels near each end. On the right lies a modern deck: its tail and nose both curve upward, and the wheels sit a little farther in from the ends. Run a finger along each one from front to back.
look.prompt: Where would your back foot go on each board to tip the nose up? Which board gives the foot a clearer place to press, and why?

check.q: Who was granted a patent for the kicktail in 1971?
check.why: Larry Stevenson, who started Makaha in 1963, was granted the kicktail patent in 1971.

check.q: What shape were most skateboard decks in the early 1960s?
choices: Kicked up only at the nose
check.why: Most early decks were flat; the kicktail came later.

check.q: What is a kicktail?
choices: A wheel set at the back of the board
A tail that bends upward at the back of the deck
A kick that pushes the board forward
check.why: A kicktail is the upturned back end of the deck that the foot can press like a lever.

lessons.title: Why the Angle Helps
lessons.mainIdea: An upturned tail starts higher, so the board can turn farther before the tail hits the ground, and the foot finds it easily.
reading: Look at a board from the side. The deck rides a few centimeters above the ground on its trucks and wheels. On a flat board, the tail tip starts at that same low height. When the tail is pressed, the tip touches the ground after only a small turn. The nose cannot rise very high before the turning stops.

A kicktail bends upward, so its tip starts several centimeters higher. Pressed down, it has farther to travel before it meets the ground. That means the board turns through a bigger angle, and the nose climbs higher. The upturned shape also lets the tip strike the ground hard and fast, which makes the *pop*, the sharp crack that starts an ollie.

The angle helps the foot too. A skater can feel the bend under the shoe without looking down. That makes it easy to put the ball of the back foot in the same spot every time. Doing a move the same way again and again is how a skater builds *muscle memory*, the feel for a motion that comes from practice.

words.d: the sharp strike of the tail on the ground that starts an ollie, and the crack it makes
the feel for a motion that the body learns by repeating it many times

look.title: Measure the Swing
look.text: Lay a flat plank across a skateboard's trucks so it sticks out past the tail. Press the plank's end down until it touches the floor, and mark how high its front end rose. Now press the real kicked tail down until it touches the floor, and mark how high the nose rose. The kicked tail lets the front climb higher.
look.prompt: Explain the difference using the words pivot and angle. Why does a tail that starts higher let the nose rise higher?

check.q: Why can a kicked tail make the nose rise higher than a flat tail?
choices: Its tip starts higher, so the board turns farther before the tail touches
It moves the pivot to the front wheels
check.why: The raised tip has farther to travel down, so the board turns through a bigger angle.

check.q: What is the pop in an ollie?
choices: The front foot sliding up the board
The landing on all four wheels
The sharp strike of the tail on the ground
The sound of the wheels rolling
check.why: The pop is the tail tip striking the ground hard, with the crack that starts the ollie.

check.q: How does the bend of the kicktail help a skater build muscle memory?
choices: The foot can feel it and land in the same spot every time
It makes the skater look down
It removes the need to practice
check.why: Feeling the bend lets the foot find the same place each time, and repetition builds muscle memory.

lessons.title: Practicing the Pop Standing Still
lessons.mainIdea: A skater can learn the pop safely on grass or carpet, where the board cannot roll, before trying it while moving.
reading: Before practicing, buckle a helmet that fits snugly, wear flat shoes, and use wrist guards. Set the board on grass or a carpet so it cannot roll. Stand with the back foot's ball on the tail and the front foot just behind the front bolts. Both feet point across the board. Regular skaters have the left foot in front, and goofy skaters have the right foot in front. Both are normal.

First, bend your knees into a low crouch. Next, snap the back foot down hard on the tail, as if stomping a bug. At the same moment, start a small jump and let the front foot go light. The tail should tap the ground with a crack, and the nose should flick up. Then let the board settle and step back onto it over the bolts.

Two problems are common. If the nose barely lifts, your back foot is probably too close to the bolts, so slide it back toward the end of the tail. If the board shoots out in front of you, you are pushing the tail forward instead of straight down, so aim the stomp at the ground. Practice ten pops at a time, and rest when your legs feel tired.

words.d: riding with the left foot in front
riding with the right foot in front
a low stance with knees bent, ready to spring

look.title: One Pop, Step by Step
look.text: The board rests on grass. The back foot's ball sits on the tail tip, and the front foot sits just behind the front bolts. Knees bend. The back foot snaps down. Crack: the tail taps the grass. The nose flicks up toward the knees, then drops back down. The feet land back over the bolts.
look.prompt: Say the steps out loud in order as you picture them: crouch, snap, go light, land. Which step do you think is hardest, and how could you practice just that step?

check.q: Where does the back foot go to practice the pop?
choices: In the middle of the deck
With its ball on the tail
check.why: The ball of the back foot goes on the tail so the stomp has a long lever arm.

check.q: The board shoots out in front of you when you pop. What is the likely fix?
choices: Aim the stomp straight down at the ground
Move the front foot onto the nose
check.why: The board shoots forward when the tail is pushed forward instead of down, so aim the stomp at the ground.

check.q: Why practice the pop on grass or carpet first?
choices: The board cannot roll away there
check.why: Grass and carpet keep the board from rolling, so you can learn the motion before moving.

lessons.title: The Ground Pushes Back
lessons.mainIdea: When the tail strikes the ground, the ground pushes back up on the tail just as hard; that push is what pops the board.
reading: Push your palm against a wall. You can feel the wall pressing back on your hand. Isaac Newton described this in his book *Principia*, published in 1687. His third law of motion says that forces come in pairs. When one object pushes on a second object, the second pushes back on the first with an equal force in the opposite direction.

In an ollie, the tail tip slams down onto the ground. The tail pushes down on the ground. At that same instant, the ground pushes up on the tail with a force just as big. This upward push is called a *reaction force*. It lasts only a tiny moment, but it is large, because the tail hits fast and the hard ground does not give.

That quick upward shove at the very back of the board is the pop. It bounces the tail up off the ground and helps send the whole board upward. A soft surface, like thick grass, pushes back weakly because it squishes. That is why the pop sounds dull and feels weak on grass, and sharp on smooth concrete.

words.d: when one object pushes on another, the second pushes back with an equal force in the opposite direction
the push back from the second object in a pair of forces
Isaac Newton's 1687 book that set out his laws of motion

look.title: Newton's Third Law
look.text: Every action has an equal reaction pushing the opposite way. When two bodies act on each other, the forces they put on each other are always equal in size and point in opposite directions.
look.cite: Isaac Newton, Principia (1687), Law III, as given in Andrew Motte's English translation (1729), paraphrased
look.prompt: Name the two bodies acting on each other when the tail pops. Which way does each force point?

check.q: When the tail pushes down on the ground, what does the ground do?
choices: Nothing, because the ground cannot move
It pulls the tail down harder
It pushes up on the tail with an equal force
It pushes sideways on the wheels
check.why: By Newton's third law, the ground pushes back up on the tail with a force equal in size and opposite in direction.

check.q: In what year was Newton's Principia published?
check.why: Principia was published in 1687; Motte's English translation came in 1729.

check.q: Why is the pop weaker on thick grass than on concrete?
choices: Grass squishes, so it pushes back weakly
Grass moves the pivot to the nose
check.why: Soft grass gives way, so its push back on the tail is weaker than hard concrete's.

lessons.title: Getting Out of the Way
lessons.mainIdea: The skater must jump and pull the knees up so the board has room to rise; the board cannot lift a rider standing on it.
reading: A skateboard has no glue on its top. If a rider stays heavy and stiff on the deck, the board cannot rise, because the rider's weight pins it to the ground. So in an ollie the skater jumps. The jump starts almost at the same moment as the pop. The legs push the body up, then pull the knees toward the chest.

Pulling the knees up clears a space under the feet. The popped board rises into that space. Watched from the side, it looks as if the board is stuck to the shoes. Really, the board is flying up on its own, and the feet are staying just above it and guiding it.

This also explains a common problem. Some beginners pop the tail well but keep their legs straight. The nose comes up, then slams back down under their weight. The fix is to practice the jump on its own: crouch, spring up and tuck the knees high. Then add the pop. Falling is part of learning; if you lose the board, crouch low and roll instead of catching yourself with stiff, straight arms.

words.d: the pull of gravity on a body, found by mass × 9.8 m/s² near Earth's surface
pulling the knees up toward the chest in the air

look.title: Two Riders, One Pop
look.text: Rider A pops the tail and keeps both legs straight. The nose lifts a little, then smacks back down; the wheels never leave the ground. Rider B pops the tail and, at the same instant, springs up and tucks both knees. The board rises under Rider B's shoes, and both come down together.
look.prompt: What did Rider B do that Rider A did not? Practice the tuck jump without a board first, then describe how it feels.

check.q: Why can't the board rise if the rider stays stiff and heavy?
choices: The rider's weight pins the board to the ground
The wheels are glued to the ground
check.why: The board has nothing holding it to the feet, and a heavy rider's weight keeps it down.

check.q: What does tucking the knees do in an ollie?
choices: It clears space under the feet so the board can rise
check.why: Pulling the knees up leaves room for the popped board to rise beneath the feet.

check.q: If you lose the board during practice, what is the safer way to fall?
choices: Lock both arms straight to catch yourself
Jump as high as you can
check.why: Crouching low and rolling spreads out the fall; stiff straight arms are how wrists get hurt.

review.q: When a skater presses the tail, what part of the board acts as the fulcrum?
review.why: The board turns around the rear wheels, so they are the fulcrum.

review.q: What is the rule for torque?
review.why: Torque equals the force times its distance from the pivot, the lever arm.

review.q: A 300 N stomp lands 0.15 m from the rear wheels. What is the torque?
What does Newton's third law say happens when the tail hits the ground?
choices: The ground pushes back up on the tail with an equal force
The tail pushes harder than the ground
Gravity turns off for a moment
review.why: Forces come in equal, opposite pairs, so the ground pushes up on the tail as hard as the tail pushes down.

review.q: Why does a short drop of the tail make a big rise at the nose?
choices: The nose is lighter than the tail
The wheels push the nose up
The nose is much farther from the pivot
review.why: Points farther from the pivot move farther, and the nose is several times farther from the rear wheels than the tail tip.

review.q: In what year was Larry Stevenson granted the kicktail patent?
review.why: Stevenson founded Makaha in 1963 and was granted the kicktail patent in 1971.

review.q: What would happen if the front foot pressed hard at the moment of the pop?
choices: Its torque would fight the tail's torque, and the nose would stay down
review.why: The front foot makes a torque the other way; pressing hard can cancel the tail's torque.

review.q: Why must the skater jump during an ollie?
choices: To give the board room to rise under the feet
To move the pivot to the nose
To press the front foot down
review.why: The board cannot lift a heavy rider, so the skater jumps and tucks to clear space for it.
